questions.title: CORS Configuration in Spring Security
questions.question: What is CORS and how do you configure it in Spring Security?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **CORS = browser security policy — same-origin restriction**
- **Preflight `OPTIONS` request:** browser checks before actual request
- **`Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header:** tells browser which origins are permitted
- **Spring Security must allow CORS before auth filters run**
- **`@CrossOrigin` vs global `CorsConfigurationSource`:** controller-level vs global config
- **Red flag:** disabling CORS entirely (`allowedOrigins("*")` with credentials) — security violation

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
CORS — Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — is a browser security mechanism that blocks requests from one origin (like `https://myapp.com`) to a different origin (like `https://api.myapp.com`) unless the server explicitly allows it.

When a browser makes a cross-origin request, it first sends a preflight `OPTIONS` request asking the server what's allowed. The server responds with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` headers. If the response permits the actual request, the browser proceeds.

In Spring Security, CORS configuration must happen before any authentication filter runs — because the preflight `OPTIONS` request carries no credentials. You configure a global `CorsConfigurationSource` bean, and Spring Security applies it to all endpoints. Important: don't use `allowedOrigins("*")` with `allowCredentials(true)` — the browser rejects this combination.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: CORS — Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — is a browser security mechanism that blocks requests from one origin (like https://myapp.com) to a different origin (like https://api.myapp.com) unless the server explicitly allows it.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Important: don't use allowedOrigins("*") with allowCredentials(true) — the browser rejects this combination.

questions.title: CSRF Protection in Spring Security
questions.question: What is CSRF and when should you enable or disable it in Spring Security?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **CSRF = forges a request from a user's browser using their existing session/cookies**
- **Mitigation: CSRF token in form or header — attackers can't read it cross-origin**
- **Disable for REST APIs with JWT:** no cookies, no CSRF vulnerability
- **Enable for traditional web apps:** form-based login with sessions uses cookies
- **Double Submit Cookie:** CSRF token in both cookie and request header
- **Red flag:** disabling CSRF for a session-based web app — real security risk

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
CSRF — Cross-Site Request Forgery — is an attack where a malicious site tricks a user's browser into making a request to your API using the user's existing session credentials. The browser automatically includes cookies, so the server can't tell the request came from the attacker's site.

Spring Security's CSRF protection works by requiring a CSRF token — a random value embedded in every state-changing form submission. The server validates it. An attacker's site can't read the CSRF token from your site due to the same-origin policy, so they can't forge a valid request.

For REST APIs using JWT in the `Authorization` header, CSRF is not a concern — browsers don't automatically include `Authorization` headers. You can safely disable CSRF with `csrf.disable()`. For session-based web applications with cookie authentication, CSRF protection must be enabled.

speakable_v2.hook: CSRF — Cross-Site Request Forgery — is an attack where a malicious site tricks a user's browser into making a request to your API using the user's existing session credentials.
speakable_v2.cap: For session-based web applications with cookie authentication, CSRF protection must be enabled.

questions.title: HTTP Security Headers
questions.question: What HTTP security headers does Spring Security add and why are they important?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **HSTS:** browser always uses HTTPS for this domain
- **X-Frame-Options:** prevents clickjacking by disabling embedding in iframes
- **X-Content-Type-Options:** prevents MIME sniffing
- **CSP (Content-Security-Policy):** restricts resource loading — prevents XSS
- **Spring Security adds most by default** — know what they do, not just that they exist
- **Red flag:** not knowing that CSP is NOT added by default — it needs explicit configuration

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring Security adds several security headers by default. `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` prevents browsers from MIME-sniffing responses — forcing them to use the declared content type. `X-Frame-Options: DENY` prevents the page from being embedded in an iframe, blocking clickjacking attacks. `Strict-Transport-Security` tells browsers to always use HTTPS for this domain in future visits.

Content Security Policy is the most powerful but is not added by default — it requires explicit configuration for each application because it restricts which scripts, styles, and resources can load. A too-restrictive CSP breaks functionality; a too-permissive one provides no benefit.

For REST APIs, most of these headers are less relevant — they're browser-enforced and don't affect API-to-API communication. They matter for responses that browsers render directly.

sections.title: Concept Explained

speakable_v2.hook: Spring Security adds several security headers by default.
speakable_v2.cap: They matter for responses that browsers render directly.

questions.title: Rate Limiting and Brute Force Protection
questions.question: How do you implement rate limiting to protect against brute force attacks?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Login endpoint is primary brute force target**
- **Account lockout: lock after N failed attempts** — stored in DB or Redis
- **IP-based rate limiting: Bucket4j or Redis counters**
- **Spring Security `AccountLockedException`:** part of `UserDetails.isAccountNonLocked()`
- **Progressive delays:** exponential backoff per IP
- **Red flag:** only locking at 10+ attempts — modern brute force tools are distributed

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Brute force protection requires multiple layers. Account lockout is the first layer: after 5 consecutive failed login attempts, lock the account for a period. Spring Security supports this via `UserDetails.isAccountNonLocked()` — return false when the account is locked.

IP-based rate limiting is the second layer. Even if an attacker rotates usernames, limiting requests per IP slows distributed attacks. Bucket4j integrates cleanly with Spring's filter chain and uses token bucket algorithm — configurable requests per time window.

For high-security applications, add CAPTCHA after N failed attempts, and send email alerts for login from new devices or locations. Distributed attackers with botnets require reputation-based IP blocking via WAF or services like Cloudflare.
